steps.say: Extraperitoneal rupture is the commonest bladder injury, causing 60 to 70 percent of cases. It follows pelvic fractures that tear the bladder neck. The intact peritoneum walls off the leaked urine. Large bore catheter drainage for 10 to 14 days is the standard treatment. Most tears are sealed spontaneously within two weeks.
steps.tx: **Extraperitoneal rupture** (bladder tear leaking outside the sac) causes **60% to 70%** (six to seven in ten) of bladder injuries and follows **pelvic fractures** (broken hip ring) that tear the bladder neck. Treat with large bore urethral **catheter drainage** (bladder rest through a tube) for **10 to 14 days** (ten to fourteen days), because the intact peritoneum walls off urine and most tears seal spontaneously.

steps.say: Intraperitoneal rupture is caused by a blow to a distended bladder. The weak dome is burst open and urine is flooded into the belly cavity. Chemical peritonitis is triggered within hours. Urgent operative repair in layers is mandatory. Absorbable sutures are used for the closure. Catheter drainage is continued until healing is confirmed.
steps.tx: **Intraperitoneal rupture** (bladder tear leaking into the belly) causes **25% to 35%** (quarter to third) of injuries when a blow strikes a full bladder and bursts the **bladder dome** (weak roof). Urine floods the peritoneal cavity and causes chemical peritonitis, so urgent formal **operative repair** (surgical stitching in layers) with absorbable sutures is mandatory, followed by catheter drainage until a cystogram proves sealing.

steps.say: Cystography is performed with the bladder fully distended. At least 300 mL to 350 mL of contrast is instilled by gravity. Underfilled studies are reported as falsely normal. A drainage film is obtained after emptying. Escaped contrast is seen as flame shaped plumes. Adequate filling is required for an accurate result.
steps.tx: Retrograde or **CT cystography** (bladder X-ray with dye) misses tears when the bladder is half empty, so fill with at least **300 mL to 350 mL** (third of a litre) of contrast under gravity. Watch for flame shaped contrast plumes escaping the wall on post drainage films, because adequate **bladder filling** (full stretch) plus a drain film prevents false negative studies.

steps.say: Posterior urethral disruption is caused by pelvic ring fractures. The membranous urethra is sheared at the bulbomembranous junction. Blood at meatus with inability to void is the classic warning. A high-riding boggy prostate is felt on rectal examination. Catheter passage is avoided until imaging is completed. Blind instrumentation is known to worsen partial tears.
steps.tx: **Posterior urethral disruption** (membranous tear at the bulbomembranous junction) complicates pelvic ring fractures that shear the prostate from the urethra. Suspect it when blood at meatus, inability to pass urine, and a boggy **high-riding prostate** on rectal examination form the classic triad, because **blood at meatus** (bleeding from the external opening) never accompanies a simple contusion. Never pass a catheter blindly, because a false passage converts a partial tear into complete distraction.

steps.say: Retrograde urethrography is performed before any catheter attempt. Contrast is injected gently into the meatus. An intact channel to the bladder is demonstrated on fluoroscopy. A normal study is followed by safe catheterisation. Extravasation is managed by suprapubic diversion. Blind catheterisation is avoided whenever an injury is suspected.
steps.tx: Perform **retrograde urethrography** (dye X-ray of the urethra, RUG (bulb study)) before any catheter attempt whenever injury is suspected. Inject contrast gently into the meatus and watch it outline an intact channel to the bladder, because cannulating a disrupted urethra creates false passages. A normal study clears the way for safe urethral catheterisation, while extravasation diverts management to a suprapubic route.

steps.say: Straddle injury is caused by a perineal blow onto a narrow bar. The bulbar urethra is crushed against the pubic symphysis. Perineal bruising with blood at meatus is typically seen. The prostate is normally positioned, unlike posterior injuries. Retrograde urethrography is required for confirmation. Blind catheter passage is avoided until the study is completed.
steps.tx: **Straddle injury** (perineal blow onto a bar) crushes the **bulbar urethra** (front urine tube) against the inferior pubic symphysis when a rider lands hard. Suspect it with perineal bruising, blood at meatus, and a normal prostate position that distinguishes it from posterior disruption. Confirm with retrograde urethrography before catheterising, because blind passage through a crushed segment worsens the tear.

steps.say: A Colles fascia breach is followed by widespread urinary spread. Urine is tracked into the scrotum, penis, and abdominal wall. Spread is halted only at the thigh fascia lata. Intact Buck fascia is known to confine leaks to the shaft. Spreading extravasation is recognised by doughy swelling. Infected collections are treated by urgent diversion.
steps.tx: A **Colles fascia** (superficial perineal wrap) breach lets urine escape into the scrotum, penis, and abdominal wall up to the clavicles, stopping only at the fascia lata of the thighs. Intact **Buck fascia** (deep penile wrap) instead confines the leak to the penile shaft. Recognise spreading **urine extravasation** (urine outside the tubes) early, because infected extravasation demands urgent diversion and debridement.

steps.say: Complete distraction is managed first by suprapubic cystostomy. Delayed urethroplasty is performed at 3 to 6 months. Mature fibrosis is excised and a tension free anastomosis is created. Early primary realignment is reserved for stable selected patients. Delayed repair is associated with the best patency. Long term follow up is arranged for stricture surveillance.
steps.tx: Complete posterior distraction is first diverted with **suprapubic cystostomy** (bladder drain through the belly), then repaired by **delayed urethroplasty** (planned scar excision) at **3 to 6 months** (three to six months) once fibrosis matures. Early endoscopic **primary realignment** (railroading a catheter over wires) suits select stable patients, because delayed anastomotic repair gives the highest long term patency.
